newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish government cuts number of opinion surveys.
newsitem.headline: Spanish government cuts number of opinion surveys.

text.p: Spain's new conservative government said on Thursday it had taken political questions out of its September public opinion survey and would limit the number of future polls to stabilise the political climate.
The opposition socialists expressed outrage at the decision, saying that Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party (PP) government was trying to hide uncomplimentary data collated in September.

The chairman of the government's sociology research centre (CIS), Pilar del Castillo, told Congress that the monthly survey was not truly representative of political opinions and would be replaced by a poll published just three times a year.
"This (change) is needed to introduce a certain climate of calmness," she said.

But an official from the previous socialist administration said: "I can't believe that a government that has just arrived and that based so much of its opposition strategy on what the polls said does not want to know how it stands in public opinion."
The survey, in which 2,500 people throughout Spain were asked 40 wide-ranging questions, has tested the social and political mood of the country every month since 1979.
September's survey, due next week, had been eagerly awaited after private polls suggested that the government's popularity had waned since its election in May.

The socialists were forced into early elections after the political climate became charged with revelations of a series of corruption scandals and accusations that their government ran death squads against Basque rebels in the 1980s.
Del Castillo, who took over at the CIS after the conservatives came to power, denied that the government was manipulating the data.
"There is no attempt at manipulation or anything resembling it and frankly it (the criticism) is making a mountain out of a molehill," she told journalists.

Her predecessor, Joaquin Arango, said frequent surveys gave a better picture from a research point of view. "It is better to have an historical evolution of the poll than isolated surveys throughout the year," he said.

The socialists had campaigned on fears that the PP, as the first right-wing administration since the fascist dictatorship of General Francisco Franco ended with his death in 1975, would enforce a more repressive government.
